title: Beyond Earth
intro: Look up at the night sky — it is full of stars, planets, and the mysterious Moon. This chapter takes you on a journey beyond Earth into the Solar System, the stars, and the wonders of space.

sections.heading: Earth — Our Home
bullets: Earth is a roughly round planet covered mostly by water, with land in patches.
Earth spins on an imaginary line through its centre — the axis — once every 24 hours.
This spin causes day (the side facing the Sun) and night (the side facing away).
Earth also moves around the Sun in a path called an orbit; one full trip takes about 365 days — that's a year.
Earth's tilt and orbit cause seasons.

sections.heading: The Moon
bullets: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite — it orbits around Earth.
It takes about 27 days for the Moon to circle Earth once.
The Moon doesn't make its own light; it reflects sunlight, which is why we see it.
As the Moon moves, we see different lit-up portions — these are the phases (new moon, crescent, half, full).
Astronauts have walked on the Moon; it has dust, mountains, and craters made by old impacts.

sections.heading: The Sun and the Solar System
bullets: The Sun is our nearest star — a giant glowing ball of hot gas.
Eight planets orbit around the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars are smaller and rocky; Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune are bigger and made mostly of gas.
Many planets have their own moons — Jupiter has dozens.
Asteroids (rocky chunks) and comets (icy bodies with tails) also orbit the Sun.
Together, the Sun and everything orbiting it make up the Solar System.

sections.heading: Stars and Constellations
bullets: Stars are huge, distant balls of glowing gas — most are like our Sun.
Stars look small only because they are very far away.
Constellations are patterns of stars in the sky that people have given names to — Ursa Major (Saptarishi), Orion, Cassiopeia.
The Saptarishi (Big Dipper) helps us find the North Star (Pole Star).
Stars seem to twinkle because their light passes through Earth's moving atmosphere; planets shine more steadily.

sections.heading: Day, Night, and Seasons
bullets: Earth's rotation on its axis (one full turn in 24 hours) causes day and night.
Different parts of the world have day and night at different clock-times.
Earth's axis is tilted, so as Earth orbits the Sun, different parts get more or less direct sunlight.
This tilt brings the four seasons — summer, autumn, winter, spring — but the timing changes by hemisphere.
Near the equator, day length and seasons change very little; near the poles they swing widely.

sections.heading: Looking into Space
bullets: Telescopes magnify distant objects so we can see craters on the Moon, rings of Saturn, and far-away stars.
India's space agency ISRO has launched satellites for weather, communications, and TV.
Satellites orbit Earth and send back images and signals.
Space probes travel deep into the Solar System; ISRO's Mangalyaan studied Mars, and Chandrayaan landed near the Moon's south pole.
Astronauts (like Rakesh Sharma and Sunita Williams) have travelled into space.

sections.heading: Why Study Space?
bullets: Studying space helps us understand Earth better — our weather, water, and natural disasters.
Satellites help in farming, mapping, navigation (GPS), and disaster warning.
Space exploration tells us about how planets and stars form, and even where life might exist beyond Earth.
It also inspires people of all ages — astronomy is open to anyone with a curious mind and a clear sky.

key_takeaways: Earth spins on its axis (24 hours) and orbits the Sun (365 days), giving day, night, and the year.
The Moon orbits Earth and shows phases because we see different lit-up portions over a month.
The Solar System has the Sun at the centre, eight planets, plus asteroids, comets, and many moons.
Stars are distant suns; they form patterns called constellations like the Saptarishi.
Earth's axial tilt causes the seasons.
Telescopes, satellites, and space probes have hugely expanded what we know about space.

glossary.definition: An imaginary line passing through Earth around which it spins.
The spinning of Earth on its axis; one full spin takes 24 hours.
The curved path one body follows around another in space, like Earth around the Sun.
An object that orbits a planet — natural like the Moon, or man-made like communication satellites.
The shape of the lit-up part of the Moon as seen from Earth on a given day.
The Sun and all the bodies that orbit it — planets, moons, asteroids, comets.
A large, roughly round body that orbits a star and has cleared its path of other objects.
A huge, distant ball of glowing gas that produces its own light, like our Sun.
A named pattern of stars in the night sky, like Saptarishi or Orion.
An instrument that magnifies far-away objects so we can study them.
